# Practical Exercise: A fractional factorial experiment 


## Aims of this practical exercise


In this exercise you will:

-  gain experience working with fractional factorial experiments.

## Before you undertake this exercise...


Get the necessary add-on packages:


## Crack length of welds


The objective of the experiment was to identify the significant welding parameters and to determine the optimal parameter settings which gave minimum crack length (cm).

Welding parameters	| Labels	| Low level	| High level
--- | --- | --- | --- 
Current	| A	| 110	| 135
Bead length	| B	| 20	| 30
Electrode make	| C	| X	| Y
V-groove angle	| D	| 45	| 60
Welding method	| E	| 1	| 2


``` {r}
Welding = read.csv("Welding.csv") |>
glimpse()
```


## Required

Q: Confirm the design generators (aliasing pattern) are D=AC and E=ABC; then identify the full defining relationship I=?=?=?.

```{r}
model1 = lm(Rep1~A*B*C*D*E, data=Welding)
aliases(model1)
model1 |> anova()
```

```{r}
model2 = lm(Rep2~A*B*C*D*E, data=Welding)

coefficients_clean <- na.omit(coef(model2))
aliases(coefficients_clean)
model2 |> anova()
```




Q: Determine the optimal settings of the five factors. 


```{r}
effects <- na.omit(coef(model2))

# Generate main effects plot
FrF2::MEPlot(model1)
```


```{r}
IAPlot(model1, select = 1:5)
```

```{r}
BsMD::LenthPlot(effects, yaxt = "n", ylab = "effects")

```

```{r}
DanielPlot((model2), half = TRUE)

```



## Additional

Three confirmatory trials based on the optimal settings were performed and crack lengths of 0.31, 0.46 and 0.32 mm were observed.   We should check this matches our expectations using a model for prediction purposes.

The author notes, ". Each trial condition was replicated twice to create adequate degrees of freedom for the error term." Is this actually correct? Hint: Look at the run order. It rather suggests the two reps were done at the same time.
